headline: College football’s latest arms race? A fight for the coolest ‘drone show.’
author: Noah White

paragraphs.text: Drew Martin fashions himself a bit of a thief — at least when it comes to halftime entertainment.

One afternoon a few years back, Martin, deputy athletic director at the University of Texas at Austin, was scrolling from his burnt-orange office chair when a video from an Asian soccer game caught his eye.
Something was happening in the sky.
“If it’s legal,” he recalled thinking, “I want that!”

Martin oversees brand management for one of the country’s largest athletic brands, and community relations in a college town like no other. He had shaped his school into a leader for in-game spectacles. So by that evening, he was talking with a local aerospace company, Verge Aero, that had recently started in the drone business. And not long after that, he was scheming on a whiteboard with UT’s marketing department.

Then, in the fall of 2023, as the Longhorns were walloping Wyoming, the stadium lights went out. Behind Darrell K. Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium, the Longhorn logo glowed, lit by what would become college football’s latest craze: a drone show.
“Every game is somebody’s first and somebody’s last,” he said. “So it needs to be special.”

In the big (and sometimes petty) business of college sports, schools have found their latest arms race: a battle for bigger, brighter and pricier drone light shows during night football games. Nearly two dozen Division I schools have put on shows in the past two years, including some of the country’s biggest brands: Texas, Mississippi, Florida, Texas Tech and Ohio State. They typically cost more than $100,000 for four to seven images or movements — a Longhorn at Texas, an oil drill at Texas Tech, a gator chomp at Florida.

“The thought is that you’re bringing in money via attention and fan engagement,” said Scott Linzer, a senior vice president at Skyworx Drone Shows, which has worked with such schools as Florida and Ole Miss. “From our side, it’s hard to know exactly what each school’s thinking. What I can say: It’s never been a better time to be in the drone show business.”

Mississippi’s show during last year’s first round of the College Football Playoff went across ESPN, TNT Sports and the SEC’s social media channels, reaching millions of scrollers. Since then, multiple officials at other Power Four schools said, they have flown staffers to Mississippi night games this year solely to scout its drone shows.

Schools also compete for dates, as only so many U.S. companies put on the shows, which require 300 to 700 drones. Previously, Florida and Auburn were looking at the same date for a show, multiple officials with knowledge of the situation said, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter. But one of the largest providers, Skyworx, settled with the Gators. Their deal was too good. (The terms were not announced.)

The deals, for the drone companies, can be very good. While collegiate athletic department spending balloons — Division I institutions dropped more than $20.8 billion on athletics in the most recent year of available data — it can’t all go to players, coaches and facilities. Schools are also competing to win the battle of the spectacles.

“You always want to have the most interesting thing,” said Michael Ceilley, Florida’s chief commercial officer. “And when you can cater to the fan while also generating outside interest, that’s good in every way. It’s how you keep people coming.”
And cash, too.

After the covid-19 pandemic, drone shows began popping up at professional sports, including international soccer events. While multiple schools claim to have been the first to bring drones to college football, Texas’s September 2023 show is the earliest found on social media. Mississippi had a show that November and soon gained a reputation for presentations that often featured the “Party in the ‘Sip” message former coach Lane Kiffin championed.

“We watch what other places are doing and then try to see what we can do better,” said Drew Ingraham, a Mississippi senior associate athletic director. “It’s an all-out effort between multiple of our departments, but our goal is to get creative.”
“Ole Miss, by far, is one of the best to work with,” Linzer said. “The willingness to just give anything a shot is off the charts.”

The process is relatively simple. First, you need a night game on the schedule, which is negotiated with your opponent and broadcast partners. Then schools sketch images for their drone show partner, which creates mock-ups of what their art could look like via drones.

The operating company then works with school officials to determine a campus location to lay out hundreds of drones for prep during a packed game day — no small feat in its own right. At showtime, drone pilots code the fleet, preprogramming their coordinated movements, and troubleshoot after the birds leave the ground.

Each school takes a different approach. For established national brands such as Florida and Texas, any addition to game day needs to fit a buttoned-up, specific vibe associated with the school, officials said. Elsewhere, for a fresher college football power player like Texas Tech, things are different.
“We want to stand out,” said Robert Giovannetti, a senior associate athletics director at Tech. “And our brand is recognizable but a bit friskier than everywhere else. So we decided to lean in.”

One of the school’s recent drone shows opened with an image of an oil drill, a nod to the program’s “oil money” donors, the most prominent being Cody Campbell. It had another on Thursday for its Thanksgiving night game against Texas Christian University, which featured a depiction of the state of Texas and a script “Matadors,” one of the school’s nicknames. That one was “unlike any other school’s ever,” Giovannetti contended.

About 375 miles southeast, Martin finished up Thanksgiving dinner and likely kept an eye on the in-state rival. His latest interest is pyrotechnics shot via drones, sparked by watching a stunt during Kendrick Lamar’s Super Bowl 59 halftime show and another late-night Asian sporting event. When “College GameDay” visited for Texas’s game against Ohio State earlier this year, the ESPN show opened with a smoky flash above the set. Since then, more than 10 other schools have incorporated pyrotechnics, and surely none will send credit to Austin.
No shame in the drone show game, though, when chasing the next publicity buzz.
“R and D,” Martin said with a laugh. “Rip off and duplicate.”
